title: Reflection and Refraction
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Physics
summary: The law of reflection, images in plane mirrors, and why light bends when it passes between air, water and glass — explained by the change in the speed of light.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe what happens when light reflects from a flat (plane) surface such as a mirror, and use the **law of reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. (8Ps.01)
Describe **refraction** — the bending of light at the boundary between air and glass, or air and water — and explain it by the **change in the speed of light**. (8Ps.02)

Thinking and Working Scientifically used on this page: using an analogy as a model (8TWSm.01, 8TWSm.02), taking accurate measurements with a protractor (8TWSc.04) and spotting anomalous results (8TWSa.02).

blocks.text: 2. How light travels

Light travels in **straight lines** from a source (the Sun, a lamp) until it meets something. When light hits a surface, three things can happen: it can be **reflected** (bounce off), **absorbed** (taken in, which warms the surface), or **transmitted** (pass through, as with glass or water). Often more than one happens at once — a window lets most light through but you can still see a faint reflection in it.

We show the path of light with **rays**: straight lines drawn with a ruler, with an **arrow** showing which way the light is going. An arrow pointing the wrong way loses marks in Checkpoint-style questions.
3. Reflection at a plane mirror
To describe reflection we always draw the **normal**: a dashed line at **90°** to the mirror, at the point where the ray hits it. Both angles are measured **from the normal**, never from the mirror.

blocks.title: The law of reflection
items: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection** (i = r)
The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the **same flat plane** (the same flat sheet of paper).
A ray that hits the mirror **along the normal** (i = 0°) is reflected straight back along the same line.

blocks.text: **Measuring from the mirror — the classic trap.** If a question tells you the angle between the ray and the **mirror surface**, subtract it from 90° to get the angle of incidence. For example, a ray at 30° to the mirror has i = 90° − 30° = **60°**, so r = 60° too.
4. Smooth and rough surfaces
Every surface obeys the law of reflection. What changes is how flat the surface is.

blocks.caption: Left: parallel rays hit a smooth surface and stay parallel (regular reflection). Right: parallel rays hit a rough surface, meet tiny pieces of surface at different angles and scatter (diffuse reflection).

rows: very smooth and flat: mirror, still water, polished metal
rough at a tiny scale: paper, wood, cloth, a wall
they go off in many different directions
no image — you just see the surface itself
yes, at every tiny piece of surface — each piece has its own normal

blocks.text: Diffuse reflection is why you can read this page from any angle: light from the page is scattered towards your eyes from wherever you sit.
5. The image in a plane mirror

When you look in a mirror, light from you reflects off the mirror into your eyes. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays **back** behind the mirror and you "see" an image there.

blocks.text: 6. Using reflection: the periscope

A **periscope** lets you see over a wall or out of a submarine. It has two plane mirrors, parallel to each other and each at **45°** to the tube. Light from the object hits the top mirror at an angle of incidence of 45°, so it is reflected at 45° — turned through 90° — straight down the tube. The bottom mirror turns it through 90° again, into your eye.

blocks.text: 7. Refraction — light changes speed
Light travels at different **speeds** in different materials. It is fastest in a vacuum (and almost as fast in air), and slower in water and glass.

**Refraction** happens at the **boundary** between two transparent materials. When light crosses the boundary **at an angle**, the change of speed makes it **change direction**. The rule depends on whether the light slows down or speeds up:

rows: bends **towards** the normal (angle of refraction smaller than angle of incidence)
bends **away from** the normal (angle in air is bigger)
**does not change direction** — it goes straight through

blocks.text: In the diagram the angle of incidence is 50° and the angle of refraction inside the glass is about 31°. When the light leaves the opposite parallel side it bends back by the same amount, so the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray** — it has only been shifted sideways.
Some light is also **reflected** at every boundary. That is why you see a faint reflection in a shop window while you can also see through it.
8. Why does a change of speed cause bending? An analogy

An **analogy** is a model that compares something we cannot see with something familiar (8TWSm.01). Imagine a line of students marching side by side, arm in arm, across a road and onto a muddy field, where everyone must walk more slowly.

items: If the line meets the mud **at an angle**, one end of the line reaches the mud first and slows down while the other end is still on the road, moving fast.
The fast end catches up, so the whole line **swings round** and changes direction — towards the normal.
If the line meets the mud **head-on** (along the normal), everyone slows at the same moment, so the line slows but **does not turn**.
Leaving the mud (speeding up) at an angle, the line swings the other way — away from the normal.

blocks.text: The same idea works for a toy car rolling at an angle from a smooth floor onto a carpet: the wheel that reaches the carpet first slows first, so the car turns. **Limitation of the analogy:** light is not made of marching people and has no wheels — the analogy shows the effect of a speed change, not what light really is.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
items: الانعكاس: زاوية السقوط = زاوية الانعكاس، والزاويتين بتتقاسوا دايمًا من العمود المقام (normal) مش من المرآة.
الانكسار سببه إن سرعة الضوء بتتغير لما يعدّي من وسط لوسط.
من الهوا للزجاج أو الميه: الضوء بيبطّأ ← بينكسر ناحية العمود.
من الزجاج أو الميه للهوا: الضوء بيسرع ← بينكسر بعيد عن العمود.
لو دخل على العمود بالظبط: سرعته بتتغير بس مش بيغيّر اتجاهه.

blocks.text: 9. Refraction in everyday life

Light from an object under water speeds up as it leaves the water, so it bends **away from the normal**. Your eye traces the ray back in a straight line, so the object seems to be **higher** than it really is.

items: A **swimming pool looks shallower** than it really is — a safety risk for people who jump in.
A straight **straw or pencil in a glass of water looks bent** at the water surface.
Glass **lenses** in spectacles, cameras and microscopes use refraction to bend light and form images.
A fish under water is not quite where it seems — a bird diving for it must allow for refraction.

blocks.text: 10. Investigating reflection and refraction
Both laws can be investigated with a **ray box** (a lamp with a narrow slit), a **plane mirror** or a **rectangular glass block**, a **protractor**, a sharp pencil and paper.

items: Draw a straight line for the mirror (or trace round the glass block). Draw the normal at 90° with the protractor.
Draw lines from the normal at the angle of incidence you want: 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60°.
Shine the narrow ray along each line. Mark the reflected (or emergent) ray with two small crosses far apart, then join them with a ruler.
Measure each angle **from the normal** with the protractor and record it in a table.
Repeat each angle and calculate a mean if the readings differ.

blocks.text: **Accuracy:** use a narrow ray, sharp pencil, crosses far apart, and read the protractor straight on. Work in a darkened room so the ray is easy to see. **Risk:** the ray-box lamp gets hot — do not touch the bulb, and switch off when not in use.

**Anomalous result:** a reading that does not fit the pattern. In a reflection experiment, every reflected angle should be close to the incident angle; a pair such as i = 40°, r = 48° is anomalous and should be measured again.
11. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle of incidence is 35°. (a) What is the angle of reflection? [1] (b) What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray? [1]

items: (a) Law of reflection: r = i = **35°**.
(b) The angle between the two rays is i + r = 35° + 35° = **70°**.
**Common mistake:** giving 35° for (b). The angle between the rays is made of both angles together.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A ray hits a mirror. The angle between the ray and the **mirror surface** is 25°. Calculate the angle of reflection. [2]

items: The normal is at 90° to the mirror, so angle of incidence = 90° − 25° = 65° (1).
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **65°** (1).
**Common mistake:** answering 25°. Angles are always measured from the normal.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Ali stands 1.2 m in front of a plane mirror. (a) How far is his image from the mirror? [1] (b) He walks 0.5 m towards the mirror. How far is he now from his image? [2]

items: (a) The image is as far behind the mirror as he is in front: **1.2 m**.
(b) New distance to mirror = 1.2 − 0.5 = 0.7 m (1). Image is 0.7 m behind the mirror, so distance from Ali to image = 0.7 + 0.7 = **1.4 m** (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A ray of light passes from air into a glass block. Its angle of incidence is 40°. Which could be the angle of refraction: 0°, 26°, 40° or 55°? Explain your choice. [2]

items: Light slows down as it enters glass, so it bends **towards** the normal and the angle of refraction must be **smaller** than 40° — but not 0°, because only a ray along the normal goes straight through (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Explain why a ray of light that enters a glass block **along the normal** does not change direction, but a ray that enters at an angle does. [2]

items: In both cases the light **slows down** when it enters the glass (1).
Along the normal, the whole of the light front reaches the glass at the same moment and slows together, so it does not turn; at an angle, one side slows first, so the ray changes direction (1).
**Common mistake:** saying the ray along the normal "does not refract because its speed does not change". The speed does change — only the direction stays the same.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — A student shines rays at a mirror and records these results. Identify the anomalous result and suggest what she should do. [2]

items: The anomalous result is at **i = 40°** (r = 47°): the law says r should be about 40°; the others are within 1° (1).
She should **repeat** that measurement (check she measured from the normal and marked the ray accurately) and leave the anomaly out of any conclusion (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Measuring angles from the **mirror** or the **glass surface** instead of from the **normal**.
Forgetting the **arrows** on rays, or drawing them pointing the wrong way.
Drawing rays freehand. Use a ruler and a sharp pencil.
Saying light bends because the material is "thicker" or "denser". Checkpoint wants the reason: the **speed of light changes**.
Saying light **speeds up** when it enters glass or water. It **slows down**.
Mixing up the directions: slowing down → **towards** the normal; speeding up → **away from** the normal.
Writing "reflection" when the question is about light passing **through** a boundary (that is refraction).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Label** a ray diagram: incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection.
**Calculate or state** an angle using i = r — watch for an angle given to the mirror surface (subtract from 90°).
**Complete a ray diagram**: draw the reflected ray with a ruler and protractor, or draw the path through a glass block (towards the normal going in, away coming out).
**Choose** the correct path of a ray from four options (A–D) at an air–glass or air–water boundary.
**Explain** refraction in terms of speed: "light slows down in glass, so it bends towards the normal". Name the change of speed for the mark.
**Analyse results**: find the anomalous result in a table of angles, describe the pattern, suggest an improvement.
Exam technique: if a question says "use the word *normal*" or "in terms of speed", those words must appear in your answer.

Practice

blocks.title: Reflection and refraction — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme. Give angles in degrees.

questions.q: Which statement about the **angle of incidence** is correct?
c: It is measured between the incident ray and the normal.
It is measured between the incident ray and the mirror.
It is measured between the incident ray and the reflected ray.
questions.e: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the **normal** (the line at 90° to the surface). Angles to the mirror, or between the two rays, are different angles.

questions.q: Find the angle **x**, the angle of reflection. [1]
questions.e: Law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **35°**.

questions.e: The given 20° is measured from the **mirror**, not the normal. Angle of incidence = 90° − 20° = 70°. Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **70°**. (20° is the trap answer.)
questions.p:
Question 3
A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the ray and the mirror is 20°.

questions.q: A ray of light reflects from a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 110°. What is the angle of incidence? [1]
questions.e: The angle between the rays = i + r, and i = r. So 2i = 110°, i = 110 ÷ 2 = **55°**.

questions.q: What name is given to the imaginary line drawn at 90° to a surface, at the point where a ray of light hits it? [1]
questions.e: This line is the **normal**. All angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are measured from it.

questions.q: Mona stands 1.5 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is Mona from her image? [1]
questions.e: The image is the same distance behind the mirror as Mona is in front: 1.5 m. Distance from Mona to her image = 1.5 + 1.5 = **3 m**.

questions.q: Which list describes the image in a plane mirror?
c: upright, same size, can be shown on a screen
questions.e: The image in a plane mirror is **upright**, the **same size** as the object, laterally inverted, and **virtual** — no light really goes behind the mirror, so it cannot be shown on a screen.

questions.q: Why can you see a clear image in a mirror but not in a sheet of white paper?
c: Paper absorbs all the light that hits it.
The paper's rough surface scatters the light in many directions (diffuse reflection).
Light does not obey the law of reflection at paper.
Light travels faster in paper than in a mirror.
questions.e: Paper reflects most light (that is why it looks white), but its surface is rough on a tiny scale, so parallel rays are reflected in many different directions — **diffuse reflection**. The law of reflection still holds at each tiny piece of surface, but no image forms. A mirror is smooth, so reflected rays stay together (regular reflection).

questions.q: Which line shows the path of the light inside the glass? [1]
questions.e: Light **slows down** as it goes from air into glass, so it bends **towards** the normal: the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence (45°). That is ray **B**. A goes straight on (no bending), C bends away from the normal (what happens when light speeds up) and D crosses to the wrong side of the normal.

questions.q: A ray of light passes at an angle from water into air. Describe and explain what happens to the ray at the surface. Use ideas about speed in your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the light speeds up (travels faster in air than in water). 1 mark: so it bends / changes direction away from the normal. Accept 'refracts away from the normal'. Do not accept 'bends towards the normal'. Do not accept 'because air is less dense' as the only reason.
questions.e: Light travels **faster in air** than in water, so it **speeds up** as it crosses the surface (1). Because it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed makes it **bend away from the normal** (1).

questions.q: A boy looks into a swimming pool. Explain why the pool looks shallower than it really is. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: light from the bottom of the pool speeds up / refracts as it passes from water into air. 1 mark: it bends away from the normal at the surface. 1 mark: the eye/brain traces the ray back in a straight line, so the bottom appears higher (nearer the surface) than it really is. Accept a correct labelled ray diagram for any of the marks.
questions.e: Light from the bottom of the pool travels up to the surface and passes from water into air, where it **speeds up** (1). It is refracted **away from the normal** (1). The boy's brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the ray back along a straight line — this meets a point **higher** than the real bottom, so the pool looks shallower (1).

questions.q: (a) Which angle of incidence gave the anomalous result? [1]
questions.e: Most results show the angle of refraction increasing steadily: 13, 19, 25, …, 35. At i = 50° the reading 41° breaks the pattern (expected about 31°, between 25° and 35°). It is also impossible for a refraction from air into glass to be close to the angle of incidence — the ray should bend towards the normal. So the anomaly is at **i = 50°**.
questions.p:
Question 12
A student shines a ray of light from air into a glass block and measures the angle of refraction.
Angle of incidence / ° | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
Angle of refraction / ° | 13 | 19 | 25 | 41 | 35

questions.q: (b) Describe the pattern shown by the other results, and suggest one way to make the results more reliable. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: as the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction increases (and is always smaller than the angle of incidence). 1 mark: repeat each reading (at least 2–3 times) and calculate a mean / repeat the anomalous reading. Do not accept 'use more equipment' or 'be careful'.
questions.e: Pattern: as the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction **increases** too, and it is always **smaller** than the angle of incidence (the light bends towards the normal) (1). To make the results more reliable: **repeat** each measurement and calculate a mean, ignoring any anomalous result (1).
questions.p:
Question 12
A student shines a ray of light from air into a glass block and measures the angle of refraction.
Angle of incidence / ° | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
Angle of refraction / ° | 13 | 19 | 25 | 41 | 35

questions.q: In a periscope, two plane mirrors are used. At what angle to the tube must each mirror be placed so that light is turned through 90°?
questions.e: At 45°, light travelling along the tube's axis has an angle of incidence of 45° and an angle of reflection of 45°, so it is turned through 45° + 45° = **90°**. Each of the two mirrors does this.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Law of reflection: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal** (90° to the surface).
A plane mirror gives an image that is upright, the same size, laterally inverted, virtual, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Smooth surfaces give regular reflection (an image); rough surfaces give diffuse reflection (scattered light).
Refraction is caused by a **change in the speed of light** at a boundary.
Air → glass/water: slows down, bends **towards** the normal. Glass/water → air: speeds up, bends **away from** the normal. Along the normal: no change of direction.
Refraction makes pools look shallower and straws look bent; a rectangular block shifts a ray sideways but keeps it parallel.
